title: Question 5
stem:
A steel ball on the end of a thin string oscillates with small oscillations, as shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1 (not to scale)

The displacement of the centre of the ball from its equilibrium position is $x$.

parts.label: (a)
(a)(i)
parts.text: Explain how Fig. 5.2 shows that the oscillations of the ball are simple harmonic.

markscheme_points.text: straight line through the origin shows that $a$ is proportional to $x$
negative gradient shows that $a$ is always in the opposite direction to $x$

hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling the two-part test for SHM in words and symbols. What must be true about the size of $a$ compared to $x$, and about the direction of $a$ compared to $x$?
Hint 2: Look closely at the shape in Fig. 5.2. What does a straight line through the origin tell you about proportionality, and what does the sign of the slope tell you about direction?
parts.proper_answer: Fig. 5.2 is a straight line through the origin, so $a$ is proportional to $x$. The negative gradient shows $a$ is in the opposite direction to $x$, i.e. $a = -\omega^2 x$, which is SHM.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what counts as SHM**
Think of SHM as a very strict rule for the acceleration. The magnitude of acceleration must be proportional to displacement from equilibrium, and the acceleration must always point back toward equilibrium. In symbols, $$a = -\omega^2 x$$ The minus sign is the physics - it means opposite direction to $x$.

Step 2: **Read the two features off Fig. 5.2**
The graph is a straight line that passes through $(0,0)$. That is the graphical signature of direct proportionality, so $a \propto x$. When $x$ is positive, $a$ is negative, and when $x$ is negative, $a$ is positive. That is a negative gradient, meaning $a$ always opposes $x$ and acts toward $x = 0$. Both conditions are met, so the motion is simple harmonic.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the period $T$ of the oscillations.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the ends of the line in Fig. 5.2 where displacement and acceleration are largest. Read off a matching pair $x_0$ in $\text{cm}$ and $a_0$ in $\text{cm s}^{-2}$ at the amplitude.
Hint 2: Recall how maximum acceleration is linked to amplitude in SHM, and how $\omega$ is linked to period $T$. Think of the pair $a_0 = \omega^2 x_0$ and $\omega = 2\pi / T$.
Hint 3: Combine the two relations to make $T$ the subject, then substitute your $x_0$ and $a_0$ values. Check that the $\text{cm}$ units cancel to leave $T$ in $\text{s}$.
parts.proper_answer: At amplitude, $a_0 = \omega^2 x_0$ with $\omega = 2\pi / T$. From Fig. 5.2, $x_0 \approx 1.2\text{ cm}$ when $a_0 \approx 13\text{ cm s}^{-2}$. $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{x_0}{a_0}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1.2}{13}} \approx 1.9\text{ s}$$
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick the amplitude point**
You need the gradient magnitude $\omega^2 = |a/x|$. Easiest is to use the maximum values. From Fig. 5.2, when $x_0 \approx 1.2\text{ cm}$, the magnitude of acceleration is $a_0 \approx 13\text{ cm s}^{-2}$. Any other clear point on the line gives the same ratio.

Step 2: **Link $a_0$, $x_0$ to $T$**
For SHM the defining equation gives at maximum: $$a_0 = \omega^2 x_0$$ and angular frequency is: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ Eliminate $\omega$: $$a_0 = \left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 x_0$$

Step 3: **Rearrange and calculate**
Make $T$ the subject: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{x_0}{a_0}}$$ Units of $\text{cm}$ cancel, so no conversion is needed as long as both are in $\text{cm}$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1.2}{13}} \approx 1.9\text{ s}$$ This is a sensible pendulum period of about two seconds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: At time $t = 0$, when the displacement of the ball has its maximum value, the ball is immersed in a trough containing thick oil so that the ball is just below the surface of the oil. This results in the subsequent motion of the ball being heavily damped.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by damping.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the total mechanical energy of the ball when it has to push thick oil out of the way. Does the amplitude stay the same?
Hint 2: What type of force from the oil causes that energy change? Think of friction, viscosity and air resistance as examples of the same idea.
parts.proper_answer: Damping is the loss of energy from an oscillating system due to resistive forces such as friction, viscosity or air resistance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy is continuously removed**
An undamped pendulum would keep the same total energy and same amplitude. In oil the ball has to do work against the fluid on every swing, so mechanical energy is transferred to thermal energy and the amplitude falls.

Step 2: **Name the cause**
We call any force that opposes motion and removes energy a resistive or dissipative force. Here it is mainly viscous drag from the thick oil, plus friction at the support. So damping means loss of oscillatory energy due to resistive forces.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: line starting from non-zero value of $x$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 2T$ that is entirely either above or below the $t$-axis
curve from $t = 0$ starting from non-zero $x$ value, with both magnitude of $x$ value and magnitude of gradient continuously decreasing

hints: Hint 1: At $t = 0$ the ball is at maximum displacement. Use Fig. 5.2 to find that starting $x$ value and mark it on Fig. 5.3 at $t = 0$.
Hint 2: Recall what heavily damped means compared to light damping. Will the ball get to the other side of equilibrium and oscillate, or will it creep back without crossing zero?
Hint 3: Picture the speed as the gradient of the $x$-$t$ graph. As energy is lost quickly, what must happen to both the value of $x$ and the steepness of the curve as $t$ increases to $2T$?
parts.proper_answer: Curve starts at $x = \pm 1.2\text{ cm}$ at $t = 0$, stays entirely on one side of the $t$-axis up to $t = 2T$, with $x$ and the magnitude of gradient both decreasing continuously toward zero, showing no oscillation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start at the old amplitude**
At $t = 0$ the displacement has its maximum value, which you already found is about $1.2\text{ cm}$. So your curve must begin at $x = +1.2\text{ cm}$ or $x = -1.2\text{ cm}$ at $t = 0$. Both are acceptable because the side depends on which extreme was chosen.

Step 2: **Stay on one side - no crossing**
Heavy damping removes energy so fast that the system does not oscillate. It creeps back toward equilibrium without passing through to the other side. So from $t = 0$ to $t = 2T$ the line must remain entirely above the $t$-axis if you started positive, or entirely below if you started negative.

Step 3: **Show continuous decay**
Draw a smooth curve falling toward $x = 0$. Both the displacement and the speed must shrink. Since speed is the gradient of $x$ against $t$, the curve starts steepest and gets flatter with time. It should approach but not cross zero within $2T$, with magnitude of gradient continuously decreasing.
